Why Peak FLOPS is the Wrong Yardstick for Inference Hardwareby Lauro Rizzatti on 11-24-2026 at 6:00 am

Categories: Semiconductor, VSORA

Key takeaways ▼
Janus Looks Both Ways. AI Hardware Must Too
For a decade we have ranked AI processors by peak FLOPS. The bigger the compute engine, the better the chip. That made sense when the defining workload was training. It makes much less sense now that the economics of AI have shifted to inference, because inference is not a lighter version of training. It is a different job altogether.
The Romans had a god for moments like this. Janus, the god of transitions and doorways, is shown with two faces: one looking back, one looking forward. AI compute has the same two faces. Training looks back, learning from data whose answers are already known. Inference looks forward, using what the model has learned to answer questions it has never seen, one word at a time. The same multiply-accumulate (MAC) arithmetic sits underneath both. The hardware workloads could hardly be more different.
The first face: how a model learns
Training starts with a huge collection of text, trillions of tokens, read in batches of thousands of sequences at a time. For each batch the model makes a guess. In the forward pass, data flows through every layer, and at each position the model predicts the next token. Because the text is known, every prediction can be checked against the real answer. The gap between the two is the loss.
Then comes the backward pass. Working back through the network, layer by layer, the model calculates how much each of its billions of weights contributed to the error: the gradients. An optimizer then nudges every weight slightly to reduce the error. That is one step, repeated millions of times.
Three things make this hard:
Compute: large matrix multiplications dominate, and each weight is reused across the whole batch, so arithmetic intensity is high.
Memory: the chip must hold the weights plus activations, gradients and optimizer state, together several times the size of the model.
Scale: thousands of chips must exchange gradients after every step before any can move on, and as the cluster grows, the interconnect sets the pace.
Training has a steady, heavy rhythm, and the design goal is simple: keep the math engines busy. GPUs were built for exactly that.
The second face: how a model answers
Now consider what happens when a question is sent to an AI assistant. First, the text is cut into tokens, small pieces of words, each turned into a vector of numbers. Then comes prefill. Every prompt token is already available since they are inputs rather than outputs, so the model processes them all together in parallel, through every layer using large matrix-matrix operations. Along the way it stores a key and a value for each token at every layer, a compact summary it will need later. That store is the key value (KV) cache. At the end of prefill the model emits the first token of its answer: the moment the reply begins.
Then comes decode. The model takes the token it just produced, appends it to the sequence, and runs the network again to produce the next one. To do that it reads the entire KV cache to look back at everything so far, then adds the new token’s key and value. One token, then the next, then the next, until the answer is complete. Each step depends on the one before it: token ten cannot be computed before token nine.
Inference itself has two faces, with two very different rhythms. Prefill is one big parallel burst of computation; it keeps the math engines busy. Decode is a long chain of small steps, each one reading the whole model and the whole cache from memory; it keeps the memory busy. And in the workloads that matter most today, chatbots, coding assistants and above all agents that plan, call tools and plan again, decode is where most of the time goes.
Plenty of compute, starved for data
During decode, a processor often runs far below its peak computing capacity, not because it lacks arithmetic power, but because memory cannot deliver the data fast enough. Two numbers make the point.
Consider a popular data-center GPU with about 1 petaFLOPS of dense FP16 compute, fed by five HBM3 stacks delivering a combined 3.35 terabytes per second. Divide one by the other and the result is roughly 300. To keep its arithmetic units busy, the chip must perform about 300 operations for every byte it fetches from memory.
Now look at what decode actually gives it. At batch size one, each 2-byte weight fetched from memory is used for a single multiply-accumulate, i.e., two FLOPs, and then discarded. That is about one FLOP per byte. Three hundred possible, one used.
Batching multiple users together helps with the weights, since one fetch then serves many sequences. But each user’s KV cache is read separately and does not amortize, so long contexts pull utilization back down. In decode, bytes per second, not rated TFLOPS, set the throughput.
The KV cache turns context into a memory problem
The cache grows quietly and relentlessly, in proportion to the model’s size, the context length and the number of users served. For Llama 3.1 70B, with 80 layers, 8 KV heads of dimension 128, and an FP16 cache, that is about 320 kilobytes for every single token.
At a 128K-token context, roughly a 300-page book and now routine for agents and coding assistants, one user’s cache reaches about 43 gigabytes, more than half the size of the model’s weights in FP8. Serve four such users and the cache alone needs 172 gigabytes. Serve eight and it needs 344, almost two and a half times the 141 gigabytes of HBM on an H200, before a single weight is stored.

And decode reads all of it, for every token it generates. That is the memory wall in concrete terms: a capacity problem and a bandwidth problem at once.
Three workloads, three bottlenecks
Seen from a hardware architect’s chair, the picture is clear. Training is bound by compute and, at scale, by communication, and is measured by time to train. Prefill is bound by compute and measured by time to first token. Decode, at low batch, is bound by memory traffic; its critical resources are bandwidth and KV capacity, and it is measured by inter-token latency and goodput, the useful output delivered within the service target.

[Source: Author]Training looks like prefill. Inference, and agentic inference above all, is dominated by decode. Evaluating all three with a single peak-compute number is a mistake. A chip can top the TFLOPS chart and still be the wrong machine for decode.
How the industry is responding
There is no universal winner yet, but the responses fall into three groups:
Locality brings the data onto the chip: SRAM-heavy and wafer-scale designs deliver enormous on-chip bandwidth, but must solve capacity, often by spreading a model over many chips.
Capacity keeps large memory close: HBM and tiered SRAM-HBM-DDR hierarchies hold big models and long contexts, but deciding what lives where becomes the hard problem.
Orchestration controls the movement: compiler-directed dataflow plans every transfer in advance, and disaggregated inference runs prefill and decode on different resources, shipping the KV cache between them.
GPUs sit across all three, with unmatched software maturity but a tendency to underutilization in low batch decode.
One example of a design built around these constraints is VSORA’s Jotunn8, an inference processor that removes the cache hierarchy entirely. Caches are a bet on reuse and decode loses that bet on every token. Instead of hardware guessing what to keep, the compiler, which sees the whole computation in advance, decides where every operand lives, and a large register-file-style memory tightly coupled to the compute units holds operands at register speed. VSORA claims more than 50 percent sustained compute efficiency against theoretical peak. Whether that holds across real serving workloads is precisely the kind of question the industry should be asking every vendor.
Measure tokens delivered, not FLOPS advertised
If peak FLOPS is the wrong yardstick, what is the right one? Two disciplines would go a long way.
First, disclose the workload: model version, precision, context length, input and output mix, concurrency and serving software. Change any one and the ranking can flip.
Second, report what users and operators actually experience. For the user: time to first token and inter-token latency. Then goodput, the useful tokens or completed requests delivered within the service target, because tokens per second alone means little if the tokens arrive too late. For the operator: energy per token and cost per completed request. In modern silicon, moving a byte costs far more energy than computing with it, so architectures that move less data per token should show it here.
The wrong ceiling
We have been measuring the wrong ceiling. Peak capability tells you how much arithmetic a chip could perform under ideal conditions. It is a useful ceiling when the work is dense and highly parallel; training rewards it and prefill often does too. Delivered service shows how many useful tokens arrive within latency and power limits, and decode frequently rewards effective memory bandwidth and data movement, not peak arithmetic.
None of this means GPUs are obsolete. It means every architecture should be judged against the actual job. The processors that win the next round will be judged by sustained, useful service within latency, energy and cost limits, not by a peak-FLOPS headline.
The Romans placed Janus at every doorway, watching what came in and what went out. That is the right way to judge an AI processor: not by how wide the doorway looks, but by how many useful tokens pass through it, on time. A faster arithmetic engine is not always a faster inference engine. The critical word is sustained.
